transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-06-30
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Samira Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Li (Redwood Solutions Eng), Maya Ortiz (Autumn Analytics ML Eng), Ravi Kapoor (Autumn Platform Lead), Dana Park (CTO), Leo (data infra)

Summary (auto):
Autumn Analytics is evaluating Redwood for a mixed streaming + batch inference workload. Primary goals: p95 latency under 250ms for short streaming responses (<=128 tokens), steady-state throughput for concurrent sessions (target 600 concurrent streams), and graceful degradation for token-burst spikes (10k token/s bursts across fleet). They are leaning toward Dedicated for predictable SLOs but require VPC/on-prem option for compliance. Next: benchmark session and pricing proposal.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex (AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh this is Alex from Redwood, i'm joined by Samira and Jordan. can you hear me okay?
[00:04] Maya (Autumn): yes thanks, can hear you.
[00:07] Dana (CTO): yep good here.
[00:10] Alex: cool, quick agenda, we'll run through your workloads, go over p95 targets and concurrency, then sketch options (hosted vs dedicated vs private), then align on next steps, does that work?
[00:18] Ravi: yup sounds good.
[00:20] Alex: Maya, do you want to kick off with what you're trying to do and the traffic patterns?
[00:24] Maya: sure, so Autumn builds a real-time summarization product for financial analysts, it's basically streaming summaries while users type and we append, and also a batch nightly re-score. live product sessions are short — usually 40 to 120 tokens per response — but we keep the stream open for interactive updates. our p95 target for interactive latency is around 200 to 250ms, we measure from request to first partial token. peak concurrency we expect around 600 simultaneous active sessions in our initial region, with bursts up to 2k concurrent for earnings days. background batch jobs run on a schedule and are less latency sensitive but heavy on tokens, roughly 10M tokens per day during normal, can spike higher.
[01:10] Samira (SE): okay that's helpful — just to confirm, the 200–250ms p95 is for first-byte/first-token on streaming, not full generation?
[01:15] Maya: yes first-token. full generation can be a few hundred more ms.
[01:18] Samira: gotcha. and what model family are you evaluating? open or closed models?
[01:22] Maya: we currently run a quantized Llama-2 variant in-house for offline scoring but are exploring higher quality models for the streaming path — likely open models we can host, maybe 13B to 70B depending on perf. we also want Redwood to handle fallbacks — if Dedicated capacity is saturated fallback to hosted cheaper variant.
[01:40] Jordan (SE): quick note, for streaming p95 at 200ms we generally recommend smaller sequence-length-optimized models or shorter context, and aggressive KV cache reuse; we also pick kernels per model, and Rudwood — i mean Redwood's runtime — can do continuous batching while preserving streaming latencies.
[01:58] Leo (data infra): quick Q — how deterministic is the p95 with batching? we've seen batchers make tail latency worse.
[02:03] Samira: right, so our continuous batching is workload aware: for streaming we prioritize low-latency lanes and do micro-batching that tends to keep p95 predictable. for dedicated pools you can reserve lanes and set a latency SLO. it's a tradeoff though — higher utilization reduces cost but can push tails.
[02:22] Ravi: what about token/sec burst handling — like during earnings spokes when lots of users paste long docs and trigger long outputs, we need the system to not drop sessions but maybe degrade gracefully.
[02:31] Samira: we do a couple things — automatic fallback to lighter quantized variants, regional routing to spare capacity, and a soft-queue that preserves session context but delays generation. on Dedicated you can set a burst reserve. also we have prefix/KV caching which helps if overlapping prompts exist.
[02:50] Maya: can you give a rough sizing for 600 steady streaming sessions at 128 tokens average and p95 250ms on a 13B model?
[02:58] Jordan: rough napkin — depends on sequence length and model ops, but for a 13B optimized model, a single A100-like node in our benchmark can handle roughly 100–150 concurrent low-latency streams with micro-batching and KV reuse at 128 tokens average. that suggests 5–6 nodes for steady 600 with some headroom. for bursts to 2k you'd need burst capacity of about additional 8–10 nodes or rely on fallback hosted routes.
[03:26] Dana: is that for Redwood Dedicated? and what about cost delta vs hosted?
[03:30] Alex: yes those numbers are oriented to Dedicated reserved GPU pools. Hosted is more elastic but cost per token is higher; Dedicated you'd get better unit economics but commit to reserved capacity. we'll send a tailored cost model.
[03:42] Maya: when you say 'nodes' do you mean GPU machines or pods? our infra team cares about reserved-GPU counts and topology.
[03:49] Samira: nodes = GPU-machines in the pool. we can break it down to gpus per pool and the VM types. in Dedicated you can pick GPU types and we provide recommended mix (e.g., 8xA100-80GB or 4xH100) depending on model and quantization.
[04:05] Ravi: what about private deployment? if we need VPC or on-prem for compliance, what's the difference for throughput?
[04:11] Jordan: Private is the same runtime but you manage the infra; throughput scales with your provisioned GPUs. there is a bit more ops overhead and you may not have Redwood's managed burst headroom, unless you contract a hybrid model where Redwood backs hosted fallback.
[04:26] Maya: can Redwood run the quantized 70B? we've had mixed success with 70B quantized for streaming.
[04:32] Samira: 70B quantized can work but streaming p95 is harder; it tends to increase token time. for your 200–250ms target we usually recommend 13B or compact 30B variants unless you accept higher tails. we also have model compilation profiles that try to minimize attention overhead for shorter contexts.
[04:51] Leo: about benchmarks — can we run a token-burst test where we replay real user sessions? we have a dataset and synthetic spike patterns.
[04:57] Alex: absolutely, that's in the next steps. Samira can build the harness; we'll run both hosted and Dedicated pilot runs and share traces. ideally we do three runs: steady-state concurrency, token-burst stress, and long-batch throughput.
[05:12] Samira: for the harness we prefer k6-based load generator or our open-source client that supports streaming websockets and backpressure. if you have recorded sessions we can replay them. please note timestamps in the trace can be noisy — our metrics are token-level latency and throughput averaging plus p95 windows.
[05:33] Maya: good. also we need audit logs and KMS integration cause finance data is sensitive.
[05:38] Alex: we have SOC 2 and KMS integrations, SSO/SAML and RBAC. we'll send the security pack.
[05:44] Dana: curious about throttling and quota controls per-tenant — we have internal teams and external customers hitting same model sometimes.
[05:50] Jordan: Redwood Console supports token-level quotas, per-route limits, and per-api-key policies; you can isolate teams into different pools. also canary rollouts for model updates.
[06:02] Ravi: on the p95 measurement — are you measuring client-to-first-token or including client network? we want synthetic numbers that reflect our edge.
[06:09] Samira: we measure server-side from request arrival at the ingress to first-token emitted; for client-to-client you should add your network latencies. during the benchmark we can place load generators in your VPC/public region to approximate your edge.
[06:25] Maya: what's the typical delta between p95 first-token and p95 full-response in your experience? with 100–150 token responses.
[06:32] Jordan: it varies; first-token p95 usually 150–300ms on optimized 13B; full-response p95 scales roughly linearly with token count but streaming amortizes some overhead. so for 150-token responses total p95 might be 1.5–2x first-token depending on generation speed.
[06:50] Alex: i want to flag fallbacks: for financial events we recommend a multi-model policy — keep a high-quality model for normal and a fast-quantized variant for overloads. Redwood policy engine can shift routing automatically.
[07:03] Maya: can you tolerably lose some quality? yes during spikes we can accept a lower-quality but faster summary for up to 30 seconds. that helps.
[07:10] Samira: we'll configure quality thresholds tied to prompt/eval sets so rollback to cheaper variants only happens if quality is within acceptable bounds.
[07:19] Leo: regarding caching, our prompts have a lot of overlap — can KV cache be shared across sessions to reduce work?
[07:24] Jordan: yes, prefix caching across similar contexts helps a lot, especially for stock tickers and boilerplate text. it depends on how you structure prompts; more templating = better cache hit.
[07:36] Maya: ok timeline — we want pilot in July and production by September if all goes well.
[07:42] Alex: good, pilot week options: July 6 or July 13, we can do a live 2-hour benchmark with both hosted and Dedicated runs. which is better?
[07:50] Maya: July 6 works for infra.
[07:52] Alex: perfect, we'll lock that.
[07:54] Ravi: small question about observability — do you expose token-level traces, and can we export to our Datadog?
[07:59] Samira: yes we emit traces and metrics; Console has per-route breakdowns. we have integrations for Datadog, Prometheus, and can export logs to your S3.
[08:08] Dana: and alerts on quality regressions?
[08:11] Jordan: quality monitoring ties to evals and prompt sets; we can set regression alerts when response embeddings diverge beyond threshold.
[08:19] Maya: any blockers on security review? we'll need to run a standard questionnaire.
[08:24] Alex: we'll send the security questionnaire and the SOC2 doc; for VPC deployments the private package details are in the whitepaper link we'll share.
[08:33] Maya: great. one more on pricing: rough ballpark for Dedicated pool with 6 nodes + burst reserve?
[08:39] Alex: i'll send a tailored spreadsheet but rough order: Dedicated commitment will be lower per-token compared to hosted; depending on GPU type could be 40–60% cheaper for sustained throughput, but capital commitment varies. we'll include numerical examples.
[08:53] Leo: during benchmark please also test the streaming backpressure behavior — we had dropped ws frames previously on another provider.
[08:59] Samira: noted, our streaming client supports backpressure and we'll validate frame loss and reconnection semantics.
[09:07] Maya: cool. anything else?
[09:09] Alex: i'll recap next steps — we'll send the benchmark plan + harness link, security pack, cost model, and schedule July 6 pilot. Samira will provision test harness and Jordan will run initial profiling. Maya to share prompt sets.
[09:24] Dana: sounds good, thanks all.
[09:26] Alex: thanks, end.
